title: Pupil Premium and SEND: Learning Without Labels 2024
author: Marc Rowland
source: Unity Research School, Research Schools Network (researchschool.org.uk), February 20,
summary: Marc Rowland, writing for Unity Research School, argues against treating Pupil Premium and SEND as meaningful predictive categories in their own right, insisting instead that socio-economic disadvantage's actual effects on learning, wellbeing, and development are what schools need to understand and respond to - the labels themselves tell you very little about an individual pupil. His central and most quotable principle is "the practitioner is the intervention": rather than defaulting to bolt-on interventions or programmes, schools should prioritise ensuring staff have the support, expertise, and consistency to teach disadvantaged and SEND pupils well within ordinary classroom teaching. He lays out a ten-point strategic framework for schools, covering everything from believing all pupils can progress, to careful individualised assessment of need, to explicit caution about interventions that remove pupils from core teacher explanation and modelling - warning that fragmented, ever-changing provision can be well intentioned but problematic. In a second section, Rowland pushes back on combined categories like PPG SEND, citing Joseph Rowntree Foundation research showing poverty and SEND status increase risk of each other bidirectionally, while insisting that neither disadvantage nor SEND status equates to low attainment, and that both groups are far from homogeneous. His overall argument is a caution against unconscious bias baked into administrative labels, redirected toward individualised, well-resourced, mainstream-first teaching as the real lever for closing gaps.
points: Rowland's central reframe is that Pupil Premium and SEND are correlates of risk, not explanations of it - the actual driver of underachievement is the impact of socio-economic disadvantage itself, which the labels only loosely track.

His "practitioner is the intervention" principle argues that consistent, well-supported teaching staff matter more than any specific intervention program, reversing the instinct to solve disadvantage gaps by adding bolt-on provision.

He specifically warns against interventions that pull disadvantaged or SEND-labelled pupils out of core teacher explanation and modelling, arguing the disruption of "something different every week" can undercut the very learning it's meant to support.

Rowland cites Joseph Rowntree Foundation research on the bidirectional relationship between poverty and SEND to argue school leaders need a more sophisticated, individualised understanding than a combined PPG SEND category allows.
quotes: Children, pupils, students are not at risk of underachievement because they are 'Pupil Premium' / SEND or any other label they may be given. They are at risk of underachievement because of the impact of socio-economic disadvantage on their learning, wellbeing and personal development.
The fact that a pupil is eligible for the Pupil Premium, the fact that a pupil has SEND tells us very little about that pupil as an individual.

The practitioner is the intervention. We need to ensure that staff have the support, expertise, knowledge, and agency to support their learners. Consistent, high quality staff are critically important.
Every pupil is an individual. A focus on labels can disempower teachers and anonymise pupils.
Poorly identified need leads to poorly identified activity, which leads to weaker results and initiative fatigue. It can lead to a reactive approach to supporting learners.

Be wary of interventions where pupils miss teacher explanation / modelling. And be wary of the disruption of pupils missing 'something different every week'. This can be well intentioned but problematic.
SEND does not equal low attaining. Disadvantage does not equal low attaining. Neither of these groups is homogeneous.

Children with SEND are more likely to become poor, while children living in poverty are more likely to develop SEND. This group of children face greater barriers than their peers in experiencing a happy and fulfilling education
